notes.meaning: When the kings of the land heard how the Lord dried up the Jordan River so Israel could cross, their courage completely melted away. They had trusted the flooded river to keep them safe, but now they were paralyzed with dread. God struck terror into the hearts of Israel's enemies before a single weapon was drawn.

Before Israel marched to war, God told Joshua to make knives of stone and circumcise the men of the nation. Circumcision was a surgical mark given to Abraham's family to show they belonged to God's covenant, which was His sacred promise. This practice had been paused during the wilderness journey, so the nation needed to renew their special bond with the Lord.

Joshua obeyed the Lord right away, crafting the knives and circumcising the men at a place called the hill of foreskins. Other leaders and family heads likely helped with the work so the entire multitude could be circumcised quickly. Joshua showed that spiritual obedience to God was more important than rushing into battle.

All the fighting men who came out of Egypt had been circumcised, but they died during the forty years of wandering in the desert. Because they refused to trust God to give them the land years earlier, that whole generation was judged and never reached Canaan. Joshua had to perform this ceremony because an entirely new generation of soldiers had taken their place.

Every male who left Egypt carried the covenant mark, but none of the boys born during the long journey had received it. Moving camp frequently through the harsh desert made it difficult and risky to care for healing children. The pause in circumcision also reminded the people that the older generation had fallen under God's displeasure.

Israel had wandered for forty years until every fighting man who rebelled had died, just as the Lord had promised. God swore an oath that those who doubted Him would never lay eyes on the fertile country flowing with milk and honey. God remains faithful to bless His followers, but He also carries out His solemn warnings when people disobey.

God raised up the sons of that fallen generation, and these were the men Joshua now circumcised. They had grown to adulthood along the road without ever receiving the covenant sign. By having them circumcised at last, God showed that He was fully reconciled to this new generation and ready to give them the land.

Once the ceremony was completed, the whole army stayed in the camp resting until their wounds were fully healed. Being sore and unable to run or fight made the soldiers completely defenseless right next to their enemies. It took tremendous faith to make themselves weak inside hostile territory, trusting God alone to guard them.

The Lord told Joshua that by obeying this command, He had rolled away the shame and mockery of Egypt from His people. To remember this turning point, they named the place Gilgal, which sounds like the Hebrew word for rolling. Israel was no longer treated as a wandering group of runaway slaves, but as God's redeemed family entering their new home.

While camped at Gilgal near Jericho, the Israelites celebrated the Passover on the fourteenth day of the month, exactly as the law required. This was only the third recorded Passover in Israel's history, and their very first inside the Promised Land. Now that the men were circumcised, the families were ready to thank God for delivering their ancestors from death in Egypt.

The day after the Passover feast, the people began eating the crops of Canaan, including flat bread baked without yeast and roasted grain. Instead of relying on wilderness food, they were finally able to enjoy the rich harvest of the land God had promised them. This meal showed that God was faithfully supplying their daily needs from the soil of their new home.

The manna stopped falling from heaven the morning after the Israelites ate the food gathered from the land. God had sent that miraculous bread every single day for nearly forty years, but He ended the miracle once regular food was available. God provides extraordinary help when His people are in need, but He expects them to work and eat by ordinary means when they can.

While Joshua was scouting near the fortified city of Jericho, he looked up and saw a mysterious man standing before him with an unsheathed sword. Joshua showed great courage by walking straight toward the armed warrior to ask whether He stood with Israel or with their enemies. The drawn sword signaled that a battle was at hand, though Joshua did not yet understand who the warrior was.

The warrior answered that He had not come to take sides as an ally, but had arrived as the supreme Commander of the Lord's heavenly army. Joshua instantly fell facedown in worship, asking what orders his Master had for him. This encounter taught Joshua that the conquest of Canaan was not merely an earthly battle, but God's own holy mission.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern interpreters view this figure as an exalted archangel leading God's hosts, rather than a visible appearance of God or the pre-incarnate Christ.

notes.meaning: The Commander instructed Joshua to take off his sandals because the ground had been made holy by His presence, and Joshua immediately obeyed. This matched the exact command God gave to Moses at the burning bush years before. It assured Joshua that the very same God who guided Moses out of Egypt was now leading him to conquer the land.
